name: David Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on housing benefit claims at the city council's benefits office, on the second floor above the shopping arcade. I get in at eight, clear the overnight change-of-circumstances forms, then spend most of the day checking rent figures, payslips and tenancy agreements. Around two I'm usually on the phone to landlords chasing missing documents. I like it when a messy case finally adds up, and what wears me out is the backlog that never goes below about three hundred.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools in that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. Our team trialled a writing assistant last spring for decision letters, and I use it when a letter is fiddly, maybe twice a week. I check every line, because it once told a tenant their rent was weekly when it was monthly. I'm not an early adopter, I waited until half the team was using it before I touched it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, a few nice shortcuts and that's it. At work I'd probably joke that the robot revolution turned out to be a spell-checker. Online I wouldn't say much, I don't really post about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays about the same, which is fine by me. I'm on decent pay for this grade and I've got about nine months of savings plus an ISA (a tax-free savings account). The only real pressure is the backlog and the yearly rule changes, and those were there before AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and go for the senior caseworker post when Gareth retires in two years. I'd keep putting four hundred a month into the ISA, because Hanna and I want a deposit for a flat by thirty. I'd use the letter tool a bit more if it got better, but I wouldn't plan my life around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, to be honest. A bit flat, maybe, because part of me finds the idea of nothing changing slightly boring. But boring with a steady payslip is not a bad deal at twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is Gareth, and why does his post matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth is the senior on our team, fifty-eight, been there since paper files. When he goes, his post opens up, and it's about three thousand a year more. In a world where nothing much changes, the senior post on my team is the main thing I'd be chasing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the office itself that worries you, even with AI standing still?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The council's budget, mainly. Every year there's talk of merging our office with the one in the north of the city. If AI does nothing, the cuts still come from somewhere, but there are plenty of benefits jobs around here, so I'd find another post.

say: I'd joke that AI turned out to be a **fancy spell-checker**.
I'd say the shortcuts are **nice to have**, but the casework is unchanged.
think: My job and pay stay **secure**, and the backlog stays my real headache.
With nine months saved and an **ISA**, I'm not worried about money.
do: Apply for **Gareth's senior post** when he retires in about two years.
Keep paying **£400 a month** into the ISA towards a flat deposit.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a slight sense that nothing changing is a bit **boring**.
S0.quote: In a world where nothing much changes, the senior post on my team is the main thing I'd be chasing.
fieldNote: David frames his career around a **specific promotion**, not around technology.
His only worry here is **council budget cuts**, which predate AI entirely.
He took up the letter tool only after **half the team** did, which fits his steady style.

steps.text: Apply for the senior caseworker post when Gareth retires
Pay £400 a month into the ISA for a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need proper training, not just a login and an email. With friends I'd be honest that our team probably shrinks. I'd say the people who learn the new systems will be fine, and I'd try to be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, most of what I do is exactly the list on that card: checking, writing letters, answering people. If the software can check a payslip against a rent figure, the council doesn't need eight of us on housing benefit, it needs maybe four. I think I'm middle of the pack, so I could be in either half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd sign up for whatever AI training the council runs, even the dull online modules. I'd ask Priya, my team leader, which roles are being planned for, because I'd rather move early than be picked. And I'd push the savings up to six hundred a month for a year, just in case I end up between posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first, then more like a knot in my stomach when I think about the team meeting where they announce it. I'm not panicking, because I've got money and there are other offices. But I'd be watching every email from HR.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be in either half. What would decide that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably whether I'm seen as the one who handles the hard cases or the one who processes the easy ones. Right now I do a lot of easy ones, if I'm honest. So I'd start asking for the complex tenancy cases, the ones with three landlords and a split household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth, funnily enough, even though he's the senior. He still prints every claim and highlights it in yellow. If the job turns into checking what the software did, I can see him taking early retirement rather than learning it, and I'd miss him.

say: I'd say the council needs to give us **real training**, not just a login.
I'd admit to friends that our **team will shrink**.
think: Most of my day is **checking and writing**, exactly what this AI takes over.
I'm average, so I could land in **either half** of a smaller team.
do: Sign up for every **AI training module** the council offers in the first months.
Ask my team leader Priya which **future roles** are planned.
Raise savings to **£600 a month** for a year.
feel: Uneasy that turns into a **knot in my stomach** around restructure news.
Not panicked, because **savings** and nearby offices give me room.
S1.quote: If the software can check a payslip against a rent figure, the council doesn't need eight of us on housing benefit, it needs maybe four.
fieldNote: David is clear-eyed that his **routine work** is the first to go.
He plans to move towards **complex cases** to stand out.
His concern for **older colleague Gareth** shows he thinks in terms of the team, not just himself.

steps.text: Complete the council's AI training modules in the first three months
Ask Priya for the complex tenancy cases and future team roles
Save £600 a month for the next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say the government has to slow this down and look after the people it replaces. At work I'd probably go quiet, because everyone would be scared and nobody wants a speech. Online I might share something about a transition fund, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone within a year or two of that date. Benefits casework is reading documents and applying rules, and if AI does any thinking work as well as a person, there's nothing left for me to do that it can't. The only bit that might last is talking to someone crying on the phone, and I'm not sure the council would pay for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, before 2028, I'd start looking hard at hands-on work, because that card gives it three more years. Hanna is a physiotherapist and she's always said I'd be good at sports therapy, so I'd look at a part-time course. I'd stop the flat plans and keep the deposit money as a cushion instead, and I'd take any redundancy package they offered early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. I keep thinking about the moment I log in and my case list is empty. Hanna's job lasts longer than mine, but only until about 2031, so it's not like one of us is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three extra years for hands-on work isn't long. Why retrain for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm going to lose my desk job in 2028 anyway, three years of pay is three years of pay, so I'd rather spend them doing something with my hands. After that, I genuinely don't know, and I'd rather admit that than pretend I've got it sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the flat plans that night when you talk to Hanna?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd shelve them. We've talked about it before in a half-joking way, but in this picture we'd sit at the kitchen table and agree not to tie ourselves into a mortgage. I'd rather keep twenty thousand in the bank than own a flat I can't pay for in 2029.

say: I'd say the government must **slow it down** and protect replaced workers.
I'd share a post supporting a **transition fund**, which I normally never do.
think: My casework job is **gone** within a year or two of 2028.
Even Hanna's **physio job** only lasts until about 2031.
do: Start a **part-time sports therapy** course before 2028.
Shelve the **flat purchase** and keep the deposit as a cushion.
Take an early **redundancy package** if the council offers one.
feel: **Alarmed**, picturing logging in to an **empty case list**.
S2.quote: I'd rather keep twenty thousand in the bank than own a flat I can't pay for in 2029.
fieldNote: David sees no part of his desk job that **survives AGI**.
He uses the **three-year robot gap** as a bridge, not a solution, and says so.
Both incomes in the household are at risk, which drives the **mortgage decision**.

steps.text: Enrol on a part-time sports therapy course before 2028
Shelve the flat purchase and keep the £20,000 deposit saved
Take early redundancy from the council if it's offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them properly. At work I'd be pushing the union rep and Priya to get a plan for retraining in writing. I'm not a big union person, but I'd go to the meetings in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending as the fast one, just with time to get ready. Five years of warning takes me to thirty-two, which is still young enough to start again. I'd be less scared and more busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a proper sports therapy qualification in the evenings, two nights a week. I'd keep working at the council and keep saving, because that pay funds the course. I'd also keep using the AI tools at work, so I understand what's coming instead of guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can manage. Having a date is weirdly helpful, because I can put things on a calendar. I'd still lose sleep some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why go to union meetings now when you said you're not a union person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a written retraining deal is worth more than me asking politely on my own. In the slow version I'd sort myself out, but this is everyone at once. I'm practical about it, if a group gets a better deal, I'll join the group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy the flat with Hanna in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a smaller one, later. I'd want to see where her clinic is heading first, because physio work holds up until about 2034 here. If she's steady, we could buy something small in 2028 with a short mortgage.

say: I'd say we have a **few years** and should use them properly.
I'd push for a **written retraining plan** at work.
think: It's the **same ending** as the fast version, with time to prepare.
At **thirty-two** I'd still be young enough to start again.
do: Study **sports therapy** two evenings a week while still working.
Attend **union meetings** to push for a retraining deal.
Keep using **AI tools** at work to understand what's coming.
feel: **Anxious** but able to manage it, because a **date** helps me plan.
S3.quote: Five years of warning takes me to thirty-two, which is still young enough to start again.
fieldNote: David joins **collective action** here only because the change hits everyone at once.
The extra time turns his fear into a **calendar of tasks**.
He links the flat decision to **Hanna's job**, not just his own.

steps.text: Study sports therapy two evenings a week for a year
Go to union meetings and push for a written retraining deal
Use the council's AI letter tool daily to learn its limits
Delay buying a flat until 2028 and choose a smaller one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time if we start now. At work I'd tell the younger ones to think about their second career early. Online I'd say councils should plan this out year by year, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not sure I'd want to spend the next ten years in benefits casework knowing how it ends. I'd probably move into something with people and hands by my mid-thirties. That gives me time to do it properly instead of in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd go for Gareth's senior post anyway, because the money helps. I'd start the sports therapy course slowly, maybe one evening a week, and see if I actually like it. And Hanna and I would buy the flat, with a mortgage we could pay on her wage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and anxious mixed together. I think I'd be all right, but I'd be thinking about it every time a new tool appeared on my screen. It's a long goodbye to a job I quite like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave casework sooner than planned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the council stop hiring caseworkers, that would be my sign. Right now they replace everyone who leaves. The day they stop, I'd go full time on the new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy the flat in this version and not the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years lets me pay down a big chunk of the mortgage before anything hits. And if we size it so Hanna's wage covers it, we're safe even if I'm between jobs. In the 2028 version buying a flat would be gambling, but in the 2036 version it's planning.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough time** if we start now.
I'd tell **younger colleagues** to plan a second career early.
think: Casework has a **known end date**, so I'd move on by my mid-thirties.
I'd rather change career **properly** than in a panic.
do: Apply for the **senior post** for the extra pay.
Try **sports therapy** one evening a week to test it.
Buy a flat with a mortgage **Hanna's wage** covers.
feel: A mix of **uneasy** and **anxious**, like a long goodbye to a job I like.
S4.quote: In the 2028 version buying a flat would be gambling, but in the 2036 version it's planning.
fieldNote: David treats ten years as time for a **planned exit**, not as safety.
His trigger to leave is concrete: the council **stopping hiring**.
He sizes the **mortgage** to one income, a careful hedge.

steps.text: Apply for the senior caseworker post for the higher pay
Try a one-evening-a-week sports therapy course this year
Buy a flat with a mortgage Hanna's wage alone can cover

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because both me and Hanna get hit inside three years. What would help is the council paying for retraining while we're still employed, not after we're out. Even a year of half pay to study would make a huge difference.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the people on the other end of the phone. A lot of my claimants are already struggling to understand letters written by humans. If a machine decides their rent, I'd want someone they can still ring.

headlineQuote: Three years of pay is three years of pay, so I'd rather spend them doing something with my hands.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old** housing benefit caseworker at a city council office, living with physiotherapist Hanna.
He is **practical and steady**, using AI letter tools only after colleagues proved them useful.
With **nine months saved** and an ISA, he's calm in AI Plateau and focused on a promotion.
From Steady Disruption onward he plans a move into **sports therapy**, timed to each scenario.
He ties every big money decision, especially the **flat**, to both household jobs.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because **both incomes** in his household are hit within three years.
whatWouldHelp: Council-paid **retraining while employed**, such as a year on half pay to study.
